title: Trafficking (8 February)
hook: on Bakhita's day the Church prays against human trafficking

segments.voice: Yesterday, Leo the Fourteenth and a new industrial revolution. Your line was people before machines. What did you do with the time you took back from a screen? Day one thousand three hundred twenty.

A little girl in Sudan, out in the fields near her village, is grabbed by strangers and carried off. She's so frightened that, by her own later account, she forgets the name her parents gave her. Her captors give her a new one: Bakhita. She is sold, and sold again, from owner to owner, and she bears the scars. Years later she ends up in Italy, where she meets the Canossian sisters, is baptized Josephine, and stays among them for the rest of her life. The Church now keeps her feast on the eighth of February, and on that day it prays against the trade that took her childhood. Today's word is that trade.
screen: `A GIRL TAKEN FROM THE FIELDS.` → `SOLD, AND SOLD AGAIN.` → `JOSEPHINE BAKHITA, 8 FEBRUARY.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Bakhita is an Arabic word meaning fortunate, or lucky. Her kidnappers gave it to her. It's hard to hear that without wincing: a stolen child called the lucky one. And yet Josephine Bakhita kept the name all her life, and the Church honors her by it. Second, the turn. In Italy, when the family that held her wanted to take her away again, the question of her freedom went before the authorities, and she was recognized as free. She chose to stay with the sisters, and later became one of them. The story Catholics tell about her isn't only about what was done to her. It's about a woman who was owned and then, at last, belonged to herself, and gave herself to God. Third, the word today. Trafficking is the buying, selling, moving or holding of people by force, fraud or coercion, for labor, for sex, for profit. It isn't only a story from another century. It happens in fields and kitchens, on fishing boats, in nail salons and apartments, sometimes in plain sight. Fourth, the Church's response. On Bakhita's feast the Church keeps a day of prayer and reflection against trafficking, and religious sisters run shelters and outreach for survivors. Underneath it is Jesus in the synagogue at Nazareth, in Luke, where he reads from Isaiah that he has been sent "to preach deliverance to the captives." Catholic teaching holds that a person can never be property. Not for any price. Not for any reason.
screen: `BAKHITA: THE FORTUNATE ONE.` · `OWNED, THEN RECOGNIZED AS FREE.` · `TRAFFICKING: PEOPLE BOUGHT AND HELD.` · `A DAY OF PRAYER ON HER FEAST.` · then, large: `DELIVERANCE TO THE CAPTIVES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one sign of trafficking. Settle, and breathe. Here's one that anti-trafficking groups often point to: someone who isn't allowed to hold their own passport or ID, because an employer or a boss keeps it for them. Here's another: a worker who owes a debt they can never seem to pay off. Hold one of those signs in mind, and imagine the places you go: a restaurant kitchen, a car wash, a farm stand. You're not looking to accuse anyone. You're learning to see. If you pray, you can ask Saint Josephine Bakhita to pray for those held captive. If you don't, simply remember her name. The bell holds the time.
Trafficking. The buying, selling and holding of people by force or fraud, which the Church prays against on Bakhita's feast. Today's word.
Your line: no one for sale. Today, look up the anti-trafficking hotline where you live and save it in your phone, just in case. Day one thousand three hundred twenty.
